vignette:
She is 50 years old, North American, single, and works as a jeweler, a profession she once loved for the precision of it and the quiet concentration it required. Before the assault, her days are structured around small, careful movements: setting stones, repairing clasps, polishing silver until it catches the light just so. She has always appreciated objects that can be mended. That belief, that broken things can be restored if handled gently enough, shapes the way she moves through the world.

The assault happens late one evening after she has closed her shop. She is carrying a small case of repaired pieces to her car when a man approaches her in the parking lot. The memory of it is fragmented in the way it is for many people who survive sudden violence. She remembers the brightness of the lot lights, the smell of cold metal from the car door, the sound of her own breathing turning thin and fast. There is shouting, the pressure of hands, a violent sense of being trapped in her body while everything familiar becomes dangerous in a matter of seconds. What stays with her most is not a single image but the collapse of safety: the knowledge that she is alone, that the world has changed without warning, and that she cannot reason her way out of what is happening. Afterward, she sits on the pavement and cannot make sense of time. The jewelry case is overturned nearby, small pieces scattered across the ground like something intimate and ruined.

In the days that follow, she tries to return to work because opening the store feels like proof that life has not been taken from her entirely. Instead, the shop becomes a place full of triggers. The sound of the front bell jangling makes her jump. A customer stepping too quickly toward the counter can send a jolt through her whole body. She begins checking the locks several times before opening and again before closing, sometimes circling the block in her car before she can force herself to park. At night, she sleeps lightly and wakes at the smallest noise. When she does fall asleep, she has dreams that are not always clear but always leave her flooded with dread, as if danger is just outside the room.

She starts organizing her days around avoidance. She no longer likes to work late. She asks a neighbor to walk with her to the lot after closing, though she feels embarrassed needing that kind of company. She stops taking certain routes home because they remind her of the street where the assault occurred. She avoids parking under the same lights. She no longer lingers in the lot to admire the evening sky or chat with nearby shop owners the way she used to. Even errands feel strategic now, chosen for the shortest path and least exposure. Her world narrows quietly. She tells herself she is being sensible, but she notices that her life has become smaller and more rigid, shaped by fear.

She also notices how often her mind returns to the event on its own. While polishing a ring or sorting stones by color, she is suddenly back in the parking lot, her body responding before she can stop it. Her heart begins to pound; her stomach tightens; her hands shake enough that she has to set the tools down. She becomes irritable in ways that surprise her. A misplaced item, a customer's impatience, a phone call she does not want to answer can leave her feeling overwhelmed and sharp-edged. She is more easily startled, especially by footsteps behind her or a sudden voice at the door. Even when nothing is wrong, she carries herself as if braced for impact.

As time passes, the assault affects the way she thinks about herself. She had once been independent, deliberate, someone who trusted her own judgment. Now she doubts herself constantly. She wonders why she had been in the lot alone, whether she should have seen danger sooner, whether any of her choices made the attack possible. The questions loop in her mind, not because they bring clarity but because they keep her close to the event, as if staying alert might prevent another version of it. At the same time, she feels detached from people around her. Friends tell her she is strong, but she hears them from a distance. She can smile and make conversation, yet some part of her remains elsewhere, scanning for threat.

At fifty, she finds herself grieving not only the assault itself but the ease she had before it. She still works as a jeweler, still sets stones and repairs delicate pieces, but she does so with a vigilance that never fully lifts. The small objects in her hands are familiar; the world beyond the counter is not.
